v_first_night.title: First night in the line
v_first_night.text:
You came up the communication trench in the dark, single file, each man holding the scabbard
of the man in front. The boards rocked under your boots. There was water under them. You
could hear it slopping and couldn't see it.

Now you're on the firestep with your rifle and the dark is full of noises. Somewhere to the
left a machine gun is traversing, and the bullets come over in a long crack-crack-crack like a
lad running a stick along the park railings. A flare goes up, white, and hangs. Everything
stops. Wire, posts, a tree with no top, a boot in the wire with something still in it. Then
the flare dies and it all moves again.

The trench stinks of chloride of lime, and under the lime there's something sweet you don't
want to think about.

"Got a fag?" Duckworth's on the step next to you, whispering. "I've lost mine. I've lost me
nerve and all, but I'll settle for the fag."

choices.text: Give him one of your last two Woodbines.
choices.text_after:
He cups the match in both hands under the parapet. In the glow his face is grey and
about twelve years old. "You're a pal," he says, and coughs, and laughs at himself for
coughing.

choices.text: Tell him you've none left.
choices.text_after:
"Liar," he says, without any heat in it. You smoke one later, alone, cupped low, and it
doesn't taste of much.

v_lice.title: Chatting
v_lice.text:
Out at rest, in a barn that used to have cows in it and still has one at the far end. The
straw is warm and damp and smells of her. Everybody's chatting: shirts off, candle stubs on
upturned buckets, running thumbnails down the seams. The lice crack. [if war.mate2]Duckworth keeps count
out loud like the tally at the end of a shift.[/if]

Walter Pilling sits apart with his back to the wall. There's not a hair on his chest. When he
sees you looking he pulls his shirt back on with the lice still in it.

"I'm nineteen," he says, before you've opened your mouth.

He'll be seventeen in March. You know because his mam made the cake for his birthday and your
sister's the same week, and you ate half of both.

"Don't tell Sarge." He's whispering. "They'll send me home. Me mam'll have written already, I
know she has. Don't you tell him."

choices.text: Keep it to yourself.
choices.text_after:
You throw him your candle stub. He catches it and doesn't say thank you, and then he
starts on his seams, and after a while he's counting under his breath.

choices.text: Tell the sergeant. He's a child.
choices.text_after:
Sarge hears you out with his pipe in his teeth. "Pilling is nineteen," he says. "It says so
on his attestation, and I'm not paid to read minds." He looks at you a bit longer. "Nor
are you."

Pilling doesn't speak to you for a week. Somebody has told him.

v_letter_mill.title: A letter from home
v_letter_mill.text:
The post comes up after dark with the rations, the mailbags slung in among the bread and the
tins of bully and the jars of plum and apple. There's a parcel for you, brown paper and string
knotted three times, which is how your mother knots everything.

Socks. A tin of toffee from the Co-op. A bar of carbolic, and the smell of it in the dugout is
so like the scullery at home that you have to sit down on the ammunition box.

And a letter, two sides in pencil, pressed so hard you can read it backwards through the paper.

"Dear Son, just a few lines hoping this finds you as it leaves us at present. They have took
girls on in the card room and your father says it will be the ruin of the trade but he says
that about everything. [if war.mate1]Mrs Shaw says {mate1_first} never writes, so you tell him
from me he wants a clip round the ear.[else]Mrs Shaw has had the letter about {mate1_first}. She
has not been to chapel since and I don't blame her.[/if] Keep your feet dry. Are you eating.
Don't do anything daft. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back tonight, two sides, by a candle end.
choices.text_after:
You tell her the food is good. You tell her about the farm woman at the billet who
laughs at the way you say eggs. You don't tell her about the boot in the wire. By the time
the candle goes your hand has cramped, and you sleep better than you have since you came
out.

choices.text: Send the field postcard. Cross out what doesn't apply.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. You leave that line and strike out the rest with the stub of pencil. You
mean to do a proper letter at rest. You put the toffee in your pack and the carbolic under
your pillow, if you can call it a pillow.

v_billet.title: Eggs and chips
v_billet.text:
Behind the lines, in the village with half a church. The estaminet is somebody's front room
with a counter put in, a stove going, and a woman who knows exactly enough English: egg, chip,
beer, no, finish. You eat egg and chips off a cracked plate, the yolk running into the chips,
and the beer is thin and sour and you'd fight a man for the next one. For a quarter of an
hour the war is somewhere else.

Shaw has a letter-card on the table and a stub of pencil, and he's been looking at them both
since the eggs came.

"Will you do it for me?" Low, so nobody else will hear. "I can read all right. It's the
putting it down. I'll tell you what to say. She'll think I've gone soft, else, never writing."

choices.text: Write it for him. Every word he says.
choices.text_after:
He tells it to you slowly, looking at the stove. That he is well. That the French have
funny bread. That she's to tell his dad the allotment wants turning before the frost. Then
he stops, and you wait with the pencil, and he says, "Put that I think about her," and
goes red to his ears.

choices.text: Make him write it. Help him with the spelling.
choices.text_after:
It takes the whole evening. He holds the pencil like a shuttle he's afraid of dropping.
Allotment has two Ls; frost has one T. When it's done it's six lines and a blot, and he
reads it back to himself three times with his lips moving, pleased as a lad with a
sixpence.

v_sniper.title: The crater
v_sniper.text:
There's a place in the bay by the old mine crater where the sandbags have settled, a hand's
width lower than the rest. This morning a man from C Company straightened up in it to ease his
back. One shot. You heard it after. It went in just under his cap badge, and he sat down on
the firestep as if somebody had called his name.

They've hung a sack over the low place since. Somewhere out there, in the grey mess of stumps
and chalk behind their wire, a man with a telescopic sight is looking at that sack. He knew
where the low place was before you did.

The lads have started calling him Fritz-at-the-crater. [if war.mate2]Duckworth says it like a music-hall
turn. Nobody laughs.[/if]

choices.text: Build the low place up tonight, under the flares.
choices.text_after:
Three hours of it, filling sandbags on your knees, passing them up, the chalk cold and
wet under your nails. Every time a flare goes up you freeze with a bag in your arms like a
baby. By stand-to it's level. Your back aches all the next day and you don't mind it.

choices.text: Leave it. Duck as you pass, and tell the new men.
choices.text_after:
You duck there every time, the way you'd duck the low beam in the shed. You stop thinking
about it. That's the part that frightens you, when you notice it.

v_eve_loos.title: Moving up
v_eve_loos.text:
Three nights of marching in the rain, never in daylight. The roads are so full of men and
guns and limbers that you go ten yards and stop, ten yards and stop, and sleep standing up
against the man in front.

Now you're in the assembly trenches. Along the parapet, under sacking, are the cylinders. Big
grey iron things, rows of them. Nobody's to say the word. The officers call it the accessory.
The men from the Special Companies who look after them have their own armbands and won't talk
to you.

[if flag.gave_fags && war.mate2]Duckworth finds you in the dark and pushes a Woodbine into your hand. "I owed
you," he says. "Don't say I never pay up."[/if][if !flag.gave_fags && war.mate2]Duckworth's further down, telling the same joke
over and over to anybody who'll listen. You can hear his voice going higher.[/if] [if war.mate3]Pilling
is asleep sitting up with his mouth open, his rifle across his knees like a toy.[/if]

The company sergeant major comes round with pay books. If you want to write anything, now's
the time.

choices.text: Write a letter and leave it in your pay book.
choices.text_after:
You don't know what to put. In the end you put that you love them, which you have never
said out loud in that house, and that your mother is to have your Sunday boots mended and
give them to our Jack. You fold it small. It sits against your chest like a hot hand.

choices.text: Leave it. Writing one is asking for it.
choices.text_after:
Half the company thinks the same. Half the company is writing anyway, licking the pencils,
hiding the pages with their arms like boys in a schoolroom. You watch them and say nothing.

v_roll_call.title: Roll call
v_roll_call.text:
They form what's left of the battalion up in a field behind the old line, in the rain. The
sergeant major has the roll. He reads it in the same voice he reads everything.

A name, and somebody says "Here." A name, and nobody does, and he says it again, and then
somebody says, "Killed, sir, I saw him," or "Wounded, sir," or just nothing, and he puts a mark
and goes on.

[if war.mate1]"Shaw." "Here, sir." Albert's voice is a croak.[else]"Shaw." Nothing. He says it again. "Shaw, A." The rain on the caps.[/if]
[if war.mate2]"Duckworth." "Present and correct, sir," and somebody near him nearly laughs.[else]"Duckworth." Nothing. You stare at the back of the neck in front of you till it blurs.[/if]
[if war.mate3]"Pilling." "Here." High, like a lad answering the register.[else]"Pilling." Nothing. Nobody says he was sixteen.[/if]

It takes most of the afternoon. The field smells of trodden grass and wet wool and the cookers
going behind the hedge, and nobody eats when the stew comes.

choices.text: Answer for the men you saw fall, when their names come.
choices.text_after:
"Killed, sir. I saw him." Your own voice sounds like somebody else's. The sergeant major
nods and makes his mark, and that's the man written down, and you think: his mother will
get a letter with my words in it.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let somebody else tell it.
choices.text_after:
Somebody else does. Or nobody does, and the names go down as missing, and you stand there
with what you saw and keep it.

v_crater_again.title: Back to the crater
v_crater_again.text:
They put you back in the old line in October, by the crater, as if Loos was something that
happened to somebody else. Same sandbags. Same smell. New faces in the bays, half of them
from the drafts, lads who don't know where to put their feet.

[if flag.built_up_crater]Your bit of parapet is still level, a bit slumped, holding. You put your hand flat on it going past, the way you'd pat a horse.[else]The sack is still over the low place. It's rotted through at one corner and nobody's mended it.[/if]

On the second morning a draft lad from Rochdale stands up two bays along to look at the
sunrise. You hear the shot after.

Fritz-at-the-crater is still there. He's had the whole of Loos and he's still there.

choices.text: Show the new lads where the low places are.

b_loos_advance.title: Loos
b_loos_advance.text:
Rum at five, from a stone jar, a tot in the lid of your mess tin. It burns all the way down
and sits in your stomach like a lump of coal from the grate.

At ten to six the gas goes over. You hear it before you see it, a long hiss all down the line,
like every steam pipe in the shed letting go at once. Then the cloud comes up, white and
greenish, and leans towards their wire. Not all of it. A drift of it comes back along the
trench, smelling of pepper and pineapple and something under both that bites the back of your
throat. You pull the hood down. Wet flannel, the chemical stink of it, your own breath going
hot against the little window.

Half past six. The guns stop. In the gap a man down the bay is saying the Lord's Prayer too
fast to get to the end of it.

"Walk," says the sergeant through his hood. "Keep your dressing. Nobody runs till I say."

Beside you on the ladder is {mate}. His hands are shaking so hard the rung is ticking against
the sandbags. [if flag.told_on_pilling && war.mate3]Further along, Pilling is looking at you. He looks away.[/if]

[if war.stalled]You get your head over the top. The first wave went fifty yards. They're lying down in the chalk in rows, too straight, the way lads lie down for a photograph on the moor, and in front of them their wire is standing whole.[else]You get your head over the top. The first wave is walking into the smoke with their rifles at the port, and nobody's falling yet.[/if]

choices.text: Over the top. Walk with the wave. ({risk_push})
Go up with {mate}. Stay at his shoulder. ({risk_help})
Over, and straight down into the first shell hole. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_trench.title: Loos
b_loos_trench.text:
Their front line is a ditch of white chalk and grey men. Some of the grey men are dead. Some
have their hands up. One of them, a lad with spectacles, keeps saying the same word over and
over, and you don't know what it means, and you will never know.

Your ears have gone. Everything comes through cotton wool, like the shed when you've done a
double shift: the bombs going off along the trench to the right, a crump and a scream and a
crump, a bay at a time.

[if war.stalled]Then a machine gun opens up from the second line, straight down the communication trench, and the bombing stops dead. Men come back round the traverse fast with their heads down. One of them hasn't got a rifle any more. One of them hasn't got a face.[else]The sergeant has lost his hood and his cap and half his ear, and he's pointing. "Up the communication trench. Bombers first. Clear it. Go on, go on!"[/if]

choices.text: Round the traverse after the bombers. ({risk_push})
Stay with {mate}. Watch his back round the corner. ({risk_help})
Get down in the bottom of the trench and stay there. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_hold.title: Loos
b_loos_hold.text:
By the afternoon the rain's come in, thin and cold, and the chalk goes to paste. You're holding
a length of their trench that faces the wrong way. The firestep is on the other side, so you
stand on dead men's packs to see over.

Nobody has brought water. Your tongue sticks to the roof of your mouth. The gas has left a
taste like sucking a penny.

Shouting on the left. Then rifle fire, picking up the way rain does on the shed roof, a few
drops and then all of it.

"Stand to! They're coming back! Stand to!"

choices.text: Up on the packs. Fire till they stop coming. ({risk_push})
Keep {mate} fed with clips. Stay low beside him. ({risk_help})
Stay under the parapet. Fire blind over the top. ({risk_ground})

l_mill_1915.title: Home on leave
l_mill_1915.text:
The train's three hours late and so cold the window has frosted on the inside. When it pulls
in, the station smells of coal smoke and fish from the market platform and the wet wool of
your own greatcoat, and under all of it, home. You have to stand still on the platform a
minute before your legs will go.

Your mother has the door open before you knock. She doesn't say anything. She puts her hand
flat on your cheek, the way she did when you had the measles. Then she smells you, and takes
you straight through to the scullery.

"Get them off," she says. "All of it. They're walking."

She boils your shirt in the copper. You sit in the tin bath in front of the fire in your
father's old coat, and listen to the clock on the mantel. You'd forgotten the clock.
[if flag.wrote_home]Your letter is behind it with the rent book, gone soft at the folds.[/if][if flag.sent_postcard]The field postcard is propped against it. "I am quite well," she reads out, not looking at you. "Quite well." She doesn't say anything else about it, and it would be better if she did.[/if][if !flag.letter_mill]"You might have written," she says to the copper.[/if]

[if war.mate1]In the morning Mrs Shaw is on her step two doors up, in her shawl, waiting for you. "Is he eating?" she says. "Is our {mate1_first} eating?" You tell her yes. You tell her he's grown a moustache. [if flag.taught_shaw]"He wrote me himself," she says. "Six lines. Spelt allotment right and all." [/if][if flag.wrote_for_shaw]"He wrote," she says, and looks at you. "It were your hand." She doesn't mind. [/if]She laughs, and then puts her apron up to her face.[else]In the morning the blinds are down at the Shaws'. They've been down since the buff envelope came. [if flag.wrote_to_mrs_shaw]On the second day Mrs Shaw sends their girl round for you. She has your letter in her apron pocket, creased to rags already. She wants it all again, every bit, and you tell her, and leave out what she can't have.[else]Mrs Shaw doesn't come out, and you don't knock, and you hate yourself for it all the way to the end of the street.[/if][/if]

[if !war.mate2]The Duckworths have a black ribbon on the knocker.[/if][if !war.mate2 && flag.wrote_to_mrs_duckworth] His dad stops you at the corner, a tackler, hands like shovels. "That joke," he says. "The parson's wife." He laughs till he has to hold the wall.[/if]

[if flag.told_on_pilling && war.mate3]Mrs Pilling stops you outside the Co-op. "They told me you tried," she says. "With the sergeant. I wrote to the War Office twice." She grips your sleeve. "Thank you for trying, love."[/if][if flag.kept_pilling_secret && war.mate3]Mrs Pilling stops you outside the Co-op. "Is our Walter behaving himself?" she says. You tell her he is. You don't tell her anything else.[/if][if !war.mate3]The Pillings' blinds are down as well. Walter was sixteen.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.wrote_to_mrs_pilling] Mrs Pilling has your letter. She doesn't come out, but on your last morning there's a cake on your mother's step in a tin, and no note.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.kept_pilling_secret] You knew how old he was and you kept it for him. You'd keep it again. It doesn't help.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.told_on_pilling] Mrs Pilling sees you from her window and lets the curtain drop.[/if]

[if flag.spoke_at_roll]On Sunday after chapel a woman you don't know takes hold of your hand in both of hers. "You were the one who told them," she says. "About our Ernest, in B Company. They wrote that it were quick." You don't remember whether it was quick. You tell her it was.[/if][if flag.silent_at_roll]In the Co-op a woman is telling the girl behind the counter that her lad is only missing, that missing means a German hospital, he'll turn up, you'll see. You saw. You pay for your father's tobacco and go out without your change.[/if]

At night the quiet keeps waking you up.

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v16_tin_hats.title: Tin hats
v16_tin_hats.text:
February, and the ground's iron. Your breath freezes on the blanket round your face and in the
morning you crack it off like the skin on cold gravy.

The tin hats come up with the rations, a whole limber of them. They're heavier than they look
and they sit on your head like a basin, and the leather lining smells of somebody else's sweat
already. The sergeant says they'll stop shrapnel but not a bullet, so don't go getting ideas.

[if war.mate2]Duckworth wears his on the back of his head and calls it his Sunday best.[/if] A draft comes up the same week: Derby men, attested
last autumn, some of them older than your father, one with a cough you can hear three bays off.
They look at the old hands the way you looked at the old hands, last May.

choices.text: Show the new men how to stand on a firestep.

v16_edith.title: Edith
v16_edith.text:
Shaw has a photograph in his pay book now, between the pages where he keeps his next-of-kin.
A girl in a white blouse in front of a painted garden at the studio on Market Street, trying
not to laugh.

"Edith," he says. "Edith Holt. From the card room." He keeps it out of the wet in an oilskin
tobacco pouch. "We're getting wed. Next leave, if they give me one before Whitsun."

He's red to the ears. He keeps turning the pouch over in his fingers like a shuttle.

"Will you stand up with me? Best man. You're the one who wrote her the letters, near enough."

choices.text: Say yes. Shake his hand on it.
choices.text_after:
His grip's like a vice. "Right," he says. "Right, then." And then, because he can't think
of anything else: "She does a lovely meat-and-potato pie." It's the most words in a row
you've had out of him since France.

choices.text: Tell him to ask you after the war, when it's done.
choices.text_after:
"After the war," he says, as if he's trying the words for size. He puts the photograph back
in the pouch, and the pouch back in the pay book, carefully, and buttons the pocket.

v16_pilling_papers.title: Papers
v16_pilling_papers.text:
March, and it's Pilling's birthday, and his mam's sent a cake in a tin with SEVENTEEN TODAY
piped on it in white. Everybody in the bay reads it. Nobody says owt.

By the next morning there's a paper for him at the orderly room. His mother's written to the
War Office, and to the MP, and the War Office has finally written to the battalion. He's to go
down the line to the base, until he's old enough.

He comes and finds you behind the cook-house with the paper folded small in his fist.

"I'm not going," he says. "I'm not leaving you lot. They'll put me in a bloody bakery, and
you'll all be up here." His voice cracks on bloody, and he's furious about it.

choices.text: Tell him to go. Get on the lorry and don't look back.
choices.text_after:
He goes to the orderly room. He comes back an hour later without the paper. "They've lost
it," he says. He doesn't look sorry. He doesn't look at you either.

choices.text: Tell him it's his choice to make, not yours.
choices.text_after:
He tears the paper up small and puts the bits in the brazier, one at a time, and
watches each one catch. Then he cuts the cake with his bayonet, eight ways.

v16_eve_somme.title: The bombardment
v16_eve_somme.text:
A week of it. Seven days and nights of our guns, so many of them that the noise stops being
noise and turns into the ground you stand on. You feel it in your back teeth. You feel it in
your water. They say nothing can live under it. They say the wire will be cut.

At night the sky over their line flickers like the cinema on Bury Road with the reel slipping.
You can't sleep and then you sleep standing up.

The colonel comes round. Walking pace, he says. Keep your dressing. The guns will have done
it for you; you'll be in their third line by dinner.

[if flag.last_letter]Your letter from Loos is still in your pay book, gone soft as cloth.[/if] The company sergeant major is round with the pay books again.

choices.text: Write a letter for the pay book. A new one.
choices.text_after:
It comes out different this time. Shorter. You tell them you're not frightened, which they
won't believe, and that if it comes to it, it'll have been quick, which nobody can promise.
You tell your father he was right about the trade.

choices.text: Leave the pay book as it is.
choices.text_after:
You lie on the firestep with your eyes shut and count the guns till you lose count, and
then you start again.

v16_after.title: July
v16_after.text:
For weeks after, the men who were caught on the wire are still on it. Nobody can get out to
them in daylight and at night their snipers watch the wire. July is hot. When the wind comes
from no man's land you breathe through your mouth and it doesn't help, because then you can
taste it.

The battalion that walked out on the first of July was eight hundred men and some. The one that
answered the roll the next day you could have got in the chapel.

One night they ask for men to go out and bring in identity discs. Just the discs. So the
mothers will know.

choices.text: Go out for the discs.
choices.text_after:
Two hours on your belly in the dark, with a pair of scissors and a sandbag. You cut the
cords by feel. Some of the faces you know by feel too. You bring back nineteen. Your hands
stink for a week however you scrub them, and you scrub them till they bleed.

choices.text: Stay in. You haven't got it in you tonight.
choices.text_after:
You lie in the dugout and listen to the others go out, and come in, one at a time, quiet.
Nobody says anything to you about it, then or after.

v16_tank.title: The tank
v16_tank.text:
September. Behind the lines one evening there's a noise like the engine house at the mill when
the big flywheel's going, and something comes down the road at walking pace that you have no
word for. An iron box the size of a tram, with a gun sticking out of each side and a tail of
two wheels dragging behind it, and it stinks of hot oil and petrol and men.

The crew climb out at the end of the road, and they're grey in the face and being sick in the
ditch, and one of them's got blood running out of his ear.

[if war.mate2]"It's a loom," says Duckworth, staring. "It's a bloody loom on legs. Me dad'd have it running in a week."[else]Somebody says it's a water carrier. Somebody says it'll end the war by Christmas. The crew don't say anything at all.[/if]

choices.text: Walk round it once. Put your hand on the iron.

v16_word_from_crater.title: A letter from the old line
v16_word_from_crater.text:
A letter comes from a man you knew at the depot, who went to the other battalion. They're in
your old line now, by the crater. He writes that it's quiet. He writes that they've had three
men killed in a month, all in the same bay, all through the head, all in the morning.

"The lads call him Fritz-at-the-crater," he writes, as if you wouldn't know. "Somebody says he
was there before your lot came. Somebody says he's been there since 1914."

You fold the letter up and put it with the others. You can see the bay. You can see the sack
over the low place.

choices.text: Write back. Tell him where the low places are.

b_somme_1.title: The first of July
b_somme_1.text:
The first of July comes up hot. Mist in the valley, burning off, and by seven the sun's on your
neck. You're carrying sixty-odd pounds: rifle, two hundred rounds, a pick, rations, two
sandbags, a groundsheet, a tin triangle sewn to your pack so the gunners can see how far you've
got. It's like a sack of flour on your shoulders, and the sack has to walk.

At twenty past seven, away to the south, a mine goes up under their line. The ground lifts
under your boots like the shed floor when the engine starts. Then our guns stop, all of them,
and in the quiet you can hear a man three bays down being sick, and a bird, and your heart.

Half past seven. Whistles.

[if war.path == rifleman]You go up the ladder behind your corporal with {mate} on the next rung down.[/if][if war.path == nco]The section's yours now. Seven men on the ladder behind you, looking at your back to see when to go.[/if][if war.path == lewis]You go in the second line with the gun on your shoulder and your No. 2 behind you with the drums. Twenty-eight pounds of gun on top of the sixty.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go with the company officer, a reel of cable paying out behind you and the telephone banging on your hip. Battalion will want to know where the company is. The line has to get there with you.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You're with the bombers, a bucket of Mills bombs in each hand. Their trench is your job, if anybody gets there.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You go behind the second line with the scoped rifle wrapped in sacking. Their machine gunners are your job, if you can find them.[/if]

[if war.stalled]By the time you're up, the first line is lying down in rows forty yards out, and the noise from the ridge has started: their machine guns, the whole length of the ridge at once, like every loom in the shed starting together. Their wire is standing. Nobody cut it. It's thick as a hedge, and there are men hung up on it like washing.[else]The first line is walking, rifles at the port, and the noise from the ridge has started: their machine guns, the whole length of the ridge at once, like every loom in the shed starting together. Men go down in rows, neatly, the way washing comes off the line in a wind. Some get up again.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Get the gun into a shell hole and fire on their guns.[/if][if war.path == signals]Keep going, paying out the wire.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Run for their wire with the buckets.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Find a fire position and hunt their gunners.[/if][if war.path == nco]Take the section on at a walk.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Walk on into it.[/if] ({risk_push})

[if war.path == nco]Get your wounded into cover first.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Get the drums forward to the men who need them.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Drag {mate} into a shell hole. He's hit in the leg.[/if][if war.path == signals]Stay with the officer. He's down.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Get a wounded bomber back to the sap.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Spot for the Lewis gun beside you.[/if] ({risk_help})
Get down. Wait for the fire to slacken. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_2.title: The first of July
b_somme_2.text:
You don't remember crossing. You remember the wire: a gap a shell had blown, men crowding to it,
and the machine gun that knew about the gap. Then you're down in their trench, and it's quiet,
and it's deep, deeper than ours, with steps cut down into the chalk. At the bottom of the steps
there's electric light. Wooden walls. Bunks with blankets. A picture postcard of a woman pinned
over a bunk, and a coffee pot, and the coffee's still warm.

Then the bombs start coming over the traverse from the next bay.

[if war.path == lewis]The gun's choked with chalk. You strip the cocking handle with your fingers shaking and it goes on the parapet, facing the wrong way, and your No. 2 is gone and you don't know when.[/if][if war.path == nco]You count your men. Four. You don't know where the others are and there isn't time to know.[/if][if war.path == signals]The wire's cut somewhere behind you. You've two pigeons in a wicker basket on your back, and one of them is dead.[/if][if war.path == bomb]This is your work. A bay at a time: pin, throw, count, round the traverse after it.[/if][if war.path == snipe]In a trench the scoped rifle's a club. You leave it in the dugout and pick up a dead man's rifle with a bayonet on.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]You've lost your corporal. {mate} is with you, white as paper, his rifle shaking.[/if]

[if war.stalled]There are eleven of you. You can't see anyone else from the battalion, left or right. Behind you no man's land is a field of men lying down.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == bomb]Round the traverse with the bombs.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Clear the gun and hose the next bay.[/if][if war.path == nco]Lead the four of them round the traverse.[/if][if war.path == rifleman || war.path == signals || war.path == snipe]Round the traverse after the bombers.[/if] ({risk_push})
Keep the wounded together at the dugout steps. ({risk_help})
Get down into the dugout entrance and stay there. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_3.title: The first of July
b_somme_3.text:
The afternoon goes on and on. The sun comes round and the trench fills with heat and flies.
You've drunk your water. You've drunk the water of the dead man by the steps. Your lips have
split and your tongue's a strip of leather.

Nobody's coming. Every time anyone puts his head over the back, towards our line, the machine
guns open up on no man's land again, and no man's land is full of men who aren't moving, and
some who are.

[if war.path == lewis]You're on your last drum. You've been counting rounds in your head the way you'd count picks on a loom.[/if][if war.path == nco]You've four men, and a lance corporal who won't stop talking about his allotment.[/if][if war.path == signals]You let the live pigeon go with a message on its leg: cut off, need bombs and water. It goes round twice and then off the right way, and you watch it till it's gone.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You've six bombs left, and their bombers have the whole of their own trench to fetch more from.[/if][if war.path == snipe || war.path == rifleman]You've ninety rounds and a bayonet and your own two hands.[/if]

They come at you from both ends of the trench at once, about four o'clock. Bombs first.

choices.text: Up on the firestep. Meet them. ({risk_push})
Pass up bombs and clips. Keep the others fighting. ({risk_help})
Stay under the parapet. Throw blind. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_4.title: The first of July
b_somme_4.text:
Dark at last. Somebody says go, and you go, back over the parapet into no man's land.

It isn't empty. It's full. Men lying everywhere in the long grass, and the ones who are alive are
calling out. Water. Stretcher-bearer. Mother. A name, over and over, a girl's name. One of them
gets hold of your ankle as you go past and doesn't let go.

A flare goes up and everybody freezes and the machine guns sweep the field low, just over the
grass, and stop. The calling starts again.

choices.text: Get up and run for our wire. ({risk_push})
Bring in the man who has your ankle. ({risk_help})
Crawl, shell hole to shell hole, as slow as it takes. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_autumn_1.title: The Somme, October
b_somme_autumn_1.text:
It's rained for a week. The ground between here and the next ridge isn't ground any more, it's
porridge with things in it. Your puttees are clay to the knee and the clay weighs more than
your boots.

On the right one of the new tanks is going forward, slow as a cart, rocking like a boat. It
noses down into a shell hole, and stops, and sits there tilted with its tail in the air,
smoking. Nobody climbs out.

[if war.path == lewis]The gun's wrapped in a groundsheet against the wet and it'll jam the moment it comes out.[/if][if war.path == signals]Nobody has even tried to run a wire across this. It's runners or nothing.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section is three old hands and four lads from the last draft, who've never been over.[/if][if war.path == bomb]The bombs are wet. Half of them won't go.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You can't see fifty yards in this rain.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]{mate} goes in to the waist in the first ten yards and you haul him out by his webbing.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The first wave's stuck in the mud forty yards out, going nowhere, and they're being shot where they stand.[else]Whistles. Up and over, and the mud takes your boot off on the first step.[/if]

choices.text: Keep going. Get across before you sink. ({risk_push})
Haul out the men who are stuck. ({risk_help})
Get down in a shell hole, water or not. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_autumn_2.title: The Somme, October
b_somme_autumn_2.text:
Their trench, when you get to it, is mostly water, with duckboards floating in it and a dead man
floating face down among the duckboards. The Germans in it are as wet and as filthy as you are.
Some of them want to surrender and some of them don't, and you can't tell which from their faces.

Somebody's bombing up the trench towards you, steady, a bay at a time.

choices.text: Go to meet them round the traverse. ({risk_push})
Get the prisoners down and the wounded out of the water. ({risk_help})
Get down behind the traverse and hold it. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_autumn_3.title: The Somme, October
b_somme_autumn_3.text:
Night, and the rain again, and they come back at you out of it. You only see them by the flashes:
a helmet, a face, a man with his mouth open, gone. You fire at where the last flash was. Your
hands are so cold you can't feel the bolt.

choices.text: Stand up in the water and fire. ({risk_push})
Keep the new lads firing. Load for them. ({risk_help})
Stay down in the water and fire over the top. ({risk_ground})

l_mill_1916.title: Home on leave
l_mill_1916.text:
December again, the second one. The town's quieter than you remember, and it takes you till the
end of the station road to work out why. There are women everywhere: on the trams, in the
railway yard in men's caps, coming off shift at the mill with their hair tied up in scarves.
And every third house has its blinds down.

July came here too. It came in August, mostly, in buff envelopes, a street at a time. Your
mother says Mrs Ormerod had two in one week.

[if war.mate1 && flag.best_man]Shaw and Edith were wed in October on his leave. You weren't there. He had his cousin stand up with him instead. Edith shows you the photograph and says, "He kept your place," and you don't know what to say to that.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.after_the_war]Edith Holt stops you on Market Street. "Has he said anything?" she says. "About after?" You tell her he has. You don't tell her he's waiting till it's over.[/if][if !war.mate1]Edith Holt is in black, though they weren't wed. Nobody tells her she can't be.[/if]

[if war.mate3]Mrs Pilling has a new hat. [if flag.urged_pilling_go]"They lost the papers," she says, "can you credit it," and looks at you as if she knows exactly who didn't lose them.[/if][if flag.let_pilling_stay]"He wrote me," she says. "He says he's needed." She says it with her mouth tight, proud and furious at once.[/if][/if][if !war.mate3]The Pillings have taken in a lodger, a Belgian. Mrs Pilling doesn't go out.[/if]

[if flag.brought_discs]Somewhere in this town a mother has a disc on a cord that you cut by feel in the dark. You'll never know which one. You look at every woman in black at chapel and wonder.[/if]

Your mother took your father to see the Somme film at the Hippodrome in the summer. She tells you
about it at tea: the guns, the men going over, the wounded smiling at the camera. She wants to
know if it's like that. You say yes.

In September a Zeppelin came over in the night and bombed Bolton. Your father went up on the
roof to watch. You can hear the pride in his voice, telling it.

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

x_fallen_shaw.title: Albert Shaw
x_fallen_shaw.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}, three yards from you. Shaw sits down the way a man sits on a step at the end of a shift, and puts his hand flat on his chest, and looks at it.

"Oh, hell," he says. "Oh, me mam."

You get to him. You get your field dressing out with your teeth. There's nowhere to put it that would be any use. He's looking past you at something, and then he isn't looking at anything.

Somebody pulls you off him. You've got him to the elbows and it's going cold already, sticky, and it smells like the back of the butcher's on Bury Road.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. Shaw. Killed {fallen_where}. The man who tells you says it quickly, to get it said, and goes.

You sit on the firestep with the bread under your arm.[if flag.wrote_for_shaw] His mother's last letter from him was in your handwriting. The next one will be in an officer's, and she'll know the difference.[/if][/if]

His mother lives two doors up from yours.

choices.text: Write to Mrs Shaw yourself, tonight.
choices.text_after:
It takes you till stand-to. You put that he didn't suffer, which you don't know. You put
that he talked about her, which is true.

choices.text: Leave it to the officer's letter. You can't.

x_fallen_duckworth.title: Harry Duckworth
x_fallen_duckworth.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Duckworth's halfway through a joke, the one about the tackler and the parson's wife, and then he isn't. There's no sound to it that you can pick out from all the other noise. He's just down, face first, with his rifle under him, and when you turn him over the joke's still on his face.

You stay with him longer than you should. Somebody has to kick your boot.[else]Somebody tells you at the water cart. Duckworth. Killed {fallen_where}.

"He wouldn't have known a thing," they say. You hope it's true. You hope it hard, like a prayer, standing there with the water tins.[/if]

choices.text: Write to his mam and dad yourself.
choices.text_after:
You tell them about the Woodbines on the first night, and the jokes, all of them, even the
one about the parson's wife, because his dad will laugh at that one and his mam will pretend
she didn't hear.

choices.text: Leave it. You wouldn't know what to put.

x_fallen_pilling.title: Walter Pilling
x_fallen_pilling.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Pilling's next to you and then he's in the bottom of the trench, curled up small, calling for his mam in a voice you've not heard out of him since he was nine and fell off the canal wall.

You hold his hand. It's all there is. His grip goes tight, tighter, like a child's at the fair when the crowd closes in, and then it doesn't.[else]The post comes up and there's a letter for Pilling, from his mam, in her careful round hand. The corporal gives it to you because you're from the same street. Pilling was killed {fallen_where} two days since.

You don't open it. You put it inside your tunic, and you can feel it there all night, square and stiff against your chest.[/if]

[if war.stage == 1]He was sixteen. He'd have been seventeen in March.[else]He was eighteen. He'd been telling everybody since March.[/if][if flag.told_on_pilling] You tried, you tell yourself. You tried.[/if]

choices.text: Write to Mrs Pilling. Tell her about the birthday cakes.
Leave it. She'll have the official letter.

x_wound_light.title: Hit
x_wound_light.text:
Hit {wound_where}.

It's like a cricket bat across the shoulder, hard, and you're sat down in the muck before you
know why. Then the heat comes, and the wet. There's a hole in your sleeve you could put your
thumb in.

"You lucky sod," somebody says, crouching over you. "That's not even a Blighty one."

The stretcher-bearers have worse to carry. You walk, down the communication trench with your
arm held against you like a parcel, to the aid post in a cellar. It smells of iodine and
paraffin and blood gone cold. The doctor looks for four seconds. Iodine that makes you shout,
a dressing, a label tied to your tunic button. A week behind the lines, maybe two. Then back.

choices.text: Go down the line.

x_wound_severe.title: A Blighty one
x_wound_severe.text:
Hit {wound_where}.

You don't remember the first part. You remember a stretcher, the bearers swearing at the mud,
the sky going past in strips between the trench walls. Morphia at the aid post, warm and heavy,
like falling asleep in front of the fire. A tent at the clearing station, a long row of you,
chloroform and wet canvas. A train with the windows painted over. A boat. The Channel's rough
and the man in the cot above you is sick all the way across, and you don't care, because
somebody said Southampton.

A hospital in England. Clean sheets that crackle. A nurse from Leeds who calls everybody "my
lad" and smells of soap. Your mother comes on the train with a cake in a tin and sits by the
bed for two hours not knowing what to say, and it's the best two hours of the war.

In a couple of months the wound will close, and they'll send you back.

choices.text: Get well. Then go back.

x_fallen.title: {fallen_name}
x_fallen.text:
{fallen_name} is killed {fallen_where}.

[if war.fallen_present]You're near enough to see it, and far enough that there's nothing to do. Afterwards you can never get the order right in your head: the noise, or him going down, or the noise again.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark, from a man who says it quickly to get it said.[/if]

You knew him before any of this. You knew his mother's kitchen.

choices.text: Go on.

c_enlist_mill.title: The drill hall
c_enlist_mill.text:
The queue starts at the drill hall door and goes back past the Co-op and round into Bury Road.
Somebody has chalked GOD SAVE THE KING on the wall, and under it somebody else has put AND OUR
ALBERT, and Albert Shaw is stood right in front of it pretending he can't read.

It's warm for September. The street smells of the mill on a hundred men at once: machine oil,
cotton fluff in their hair, the sour sweat of the weaving shed. Without the looms going your
ears feel hollow, the way they do on a Sunday.

The recruiting sergeant doesn't shout. He's like a good tackler: he doesn't need to.

"Age?"

"Just turned {age_words}, sir."

Behind you Walter Pilling is going to say nineteen. Walter Pilling was born the same winter as
your sister, and everybody in the queue knows it, and nobody says a word.
[break]
What you take with you from the shed is what you'll have out there.

choices.text: The knack you have with a loom, and legs for a ten-hour day.
The knack you have with a loom, and the voice that leads the chapel choir.
Legs for a ten-hour day, and the voice that leads the chapel choir.

c_enlist_pit.title: The recruiting office
c_enlist_pit.text:
You are {age}. The colliery band played the first lot to the station.
The manager says coal is war work too, but the queue at the welfare hall is longer than the
shift at the pithead.
[break]
What you bring from underground is what you will have out there.

choices.text: Bring digging and timbering, and stamina from a long working day.
Bring digging and timbering, and a hand with machinery.
Bring stamina from a long working day, and a hand with machinery.

c_enlist_city.title: The recruiting office
c_enlist_city.text:
You are {age}. The office manager shook your hand and said the firm would
make up your pay. The clerks are going together, a company of them, from desks all over the city.
[break]
What you bring from the office is what you will have out there.

choices.text: Bring reading and figures, and a bowler's throwing arm.
Bring reading and figures, and St John Ambulance first aid.
Bring a bowler's throwing arm, and St John Ambulance first aid.

c_enlist_farm.title: The recruiting office
c_enlist_farm.text:
You are {age}. The harvest is in and the recruiting sergeant came out to the
village on a wagon. The squire's son is taking a commission; the rest of you are taking the shilling.
[break]
What you bring from the fields is what you will have out there.

choices.text: Bring fieldcraft and a shotgun, and stamina from a long working day.
Bring fieldcraft and a shotgun, and a hand with machinery.
Bring stamina from a long working day, and a hand with machinery.

c_general.title: The last night
c_general.text:
Your mother has sewn your name into everything you own. The kitchen smells of hot iron and the
starch she's put in your collars, which the army will take off you in a week. She's not
talking much. She keeps finding things to fold.

There's one more thing you've got that the army didn't give you.

choices.text: First aid. The ambulance class at the works, certificate in a frame.
A throwing arm. Second eleven, and you can hit a stump from the boundary.
A voice. When you start a hymn, men join in.

c_training.title: Training
c_training.text:
Eight months of it. Huts with floors that never dry. Drill in your own clothes till Christmas,
then in blue serge, then at last in khaki that smells of the store and makes your neck raw.
Route marches in the rain until your feet are one blister and then they harden and you stop
noticing. Digging practice trenches in a field and filling them in again. Bayonet drill on
sacks of straw, the corporal yelling at you to scream, and you feel daft screaming, and then
one day you don't.

You learn to sleep anywhere. You learn to eat anything. You learn the men from home all over
again, the way you never knew them in the shed: who snores, who cries, who shares.

In May the orders come. France.

{section_line}

choices.text: Go aboard.

w_duty.title: A front-line tour

choices.text: Volunteer. ({duty_risk}, {duty_cost})
Keep your head down and let him choose.

w_mission.title: Your own work
w_mission.text:
[if war.path == lewis && war.take == 0]A raid is going over at two in the morning and the gun's to cover it. You set up in a sap head out past the wire with your No. 2 and four drums. The barrel shroud is so cold it burns your fingers through the mittens. When the raiders go, you fire short bursts over their heads at the German parapet, and every burst lights you up like a lamp in a window, and every German on that stretch can see exactly where you are.[/if][if war.path == lewis && war.take == 1]A German two-seater comes over low in the evening, slow and fat and close enough to see the observer's goggles. The officer wants the gun up on its post for it. You'll be standing in the open with the gun pointing at the sky and your back to their line, firing up at it while it fires down at you.[/if][if war.path == signals && war.take == 0]The line to battalion's gone again. Somewhere in the half mile of communication trench behind you a shell has cut it, and the colonel wants the company commander and can't have him. You take the pliers, a reel of D3 cable and the buzzer, and go along it in the dark, running the wire through your fingers, feeling for the break.[/if][if war.path == signals && war.take == 1]A message has to go to battalion, and the wires are all down, and the lamp can't be seen through the smoke. Somebody has to run it. Four hundred yards of open ground they've been shelling since dawn, with the message in your breast pocket in case they find you.[/if][if war.path == bomb]A bombing raid tonight: eight of you, faces blacked with burnt cork, no cap badges, no pay books, a sandbag each of Mills bombs. Into their trench, along it a bay at a time, a prisoner if you can get one, and back before their machine guns wake up.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Before dawn you crawl into the hide in the parapet, a steel plate with a slit, a sack over the slit, your observer beside you with the telescope and the notebook. You stay till dark. They have snipers looking for this plate. Some mornings you see a man over there shaving in a bit of mirror, his braces down, and he puts you in mind of your father at the scullery sink.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Down the shaft, along the gallery on your back on the trolley, to the face. Candle, the smell of wet clay and your own sweat. You lie with the listening stick against the clay and listen for them. If you can hear them digging, they're far enough off. If they stop, they're listening for you. If it goes quiet for a day, they've laid a charge.[/if]

The work's yours now. You can say you're not fit for it. You'll usually be sent anyway.

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Take the gun up.[/if][if war.path == signals]Go.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Black your face and go.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Go out to the hide.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Go down.[/if] ({mission_risk})
Say you're not fit for it tonight.

w_sick.title: Rest
w_sick.text:
[if war.take == 0]Out at rest, in a barn behind the lines. Somebody's got a mouth organ going and somebody else is
frying bread in a mess tin, and the smell of it should make you hungry. You hold your mug of
tea in both hands so the others won't see it shake. It shakes anyway. The tea goes cold and you
don't drink it.[else]Out at rest. You've slept twelve hours and you're more tired than when you lay down. Every time a door
bangs in the farmyard you're flat on the straw before you know you've moved, and the others
pretend they haven't noticed, which is kind of them, and you hate it.[/if]

The medical officer holds a sick parade every morning at seven. He's a busy man, and a tired
one, and he's seen everything.

choices.text: Report sick. The medical officer may give you a tour out of the line.
Say nothing and carry on.

w_course.title: A course
w_course.text:
The company sergeant major stops you at the water cart. There's a place going on a course,
two weeks behind the lines, and he's put your name down unless you'd rather he didn't.

[if war.course == lewis]The Lewis gun: twenty-eight pounds of it, a drum of forty-seven rounds on top like a gramophone record, and a temper. When it jams it jams in the worst place. The gun team are out of the attacks till they're needed and then they're needed more than anybody, and every German gunner looks for them first.[/if][if war.course == signals]Signals: flags, lamps, the buzzer, the field telephone and its miles of wire. When the wire's cut, and it's always cut, the signaller runs the message himself, across whatever's between him and battalion.[/if][if war.course == bomb]Bombing: the Mills bomb, pin and lever, four seconds. The bombers go first along an enemy trench, a bay at a time, and the men who come back from a bombing course don't joke about it.[/if][if war.course == snipe]Sniping: a rifle with a telescopic sight, a hide in the parapet, a partner with a periscope and a notebook. Hours of nothing. Then a second.[/if][if war.course == lead]An NCO course: map reading, fire orders, how to keep a section together when the corporal's gone. They want men who can take charge.[/if]
[if start == mill && war.course == lewis && war.mate2] Duckworth says his dad could strip one blindfold. "It's only a loom that shoots," he says.[/if]

choices.text: Take it. Two weeks out of the line, and a trade after.
Stay with the section.

w_tunnel.title: The tunnellers
w_tunnel.text:
The Royal Engineers want miners. Six shillings a day against your one, out of the attacks, and
work you know. The tunnellers do not go over the top. They go under it.

choices.text: Go to the tunnellers. You will leave the section.
Stay with the men from home.
Push on. ({risk_push})
Help the man beside you. ({risk_help})
Go to ground. ({risk_ground})

w_leave.title: Home on leave

choices.text: Go back. A stripe is waiting: the battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

e_armistice.title: The Armistice
e_armistice.text:
{ending_line}

Nobody cheers, where you are. The guns stop, and the silence comes down so hard that men look
up at the sky as if something's wrong with it. Somebody starts to laugh and can't stop. A
corporal sits down on an ammunition box and takes his boots off, both of them, right there in
the open, and nobody tells him not to.

You are {age} years old and {rank_name}, and you have been in France since you were a boy. You
can smell the wet and the cordite and the horse lines, and under all of it, for the first time
in years, nothing burning.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_posting.title: Home
e_posting.text:
{ending_line}

The war goes on without you. You read it in the paper over breakfast, like everybody else,
the long columns in small print, and you read every name, every day, and you know some of them.

Some nights you're glad. Some nights you lie awake in a proper bed with clean sheets, listening
to the rain on the slates, and you'd give anything to be in a wet bay with the lads, and you
couldn't say to anybody why.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_captured.title: Taken
e_captured.text:
{ending_line}

A boy in grey with a rifle bigger than he is takes your water bottle and your cigarettes and,
after a moment, gives you one of the cigarettes back. You walk east all day with your hands on
your head, then without, past their guns and their horses and their wounded, who look exactly
like yours.

The rest of your war is behind wire: black bread, turnip soup, work in a salt mine or on a
farm, letters that take months. Your mother gets a card in your handwriting from a camp with a
name she can't say, and she takes it round to every house in the street.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_invalided.title: Wounded out
e_invalided.text:
{ending_line}

Morphia at the dressing station, a label tied to your tunic button, a train with the windows
painted over. The hospital ship smells of carbolic and vomit and the sea. In England a woman
gives you tea with sugar in it and you cry like a child and can't stop and she just holds the
cup for you till you can.

You go home in hospital blue, then in your own clothes that don't fit. [if war.stage >= 2]A silver badge on your
lapel, so that nobody in the street hands you a white feather.[else]In the street a girl you've never seen
pushes a white feather into your buttonhole, because you're young and out of uniform, and you let her.[/if] The wound aches when it rains.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_killed.title: Killed
e_killed.text:
{ending_line}

You don't hear the one that does it. The man nearest you does, and afterwards he'll say you
made a small sound, surprised, as if you'd dropped something.

At home it comes three weeks later in a buff envelope, Army Form B.104-82: "it is my painful
duty to inform you". Your mother reads it on the doorstep with the postman still stood there,
because she knew from his face. He keeps his cap in his hands till she shuts the door.
[if flag.last_letter]

The letter from your pay book comes later, with your things: a razor, a comb, a photograph gone soft at the corners. She reads it at the kitchen table, and then she reads it again.[/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_broken.title: Shell shock
e_broken.text:
{ending_line}

It's your hands first. You look down and they won't stop, and then it's your legs, and then
you're lying in the bottom of the trench and you can hear somebody making a noise like a
kicked dog and it's you. They carry you down the line on a stretcher, though there's not a
mark on you, and you're ashamed of that the whole way.

The doctors call it neurasthenia. At home a door banging sends you under the table. Your
mother learns to close them quietly. Your father doesn't talk about it, which is how he
talks about it.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_court.title: Court-martial
e_court.text:
{ending_line}

The court sits in a schoolroom behind the lines, three officers at a table with the children's
sums still on the blackboard behind them. Nobody asks how long you'd been in the line. You
don't know how to tell them about the noise. It takes twenty minutes.

Most sentences are commuted. Most men go to prison, or back to the line under a cloud that
follows them into every bay. Your name goes in the paper at home, or it doesn't, and either way
your mother stops going to chapel.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_error.title: Lost track
e_error.text:
The war asked a question no scene answers. This is a content bug: Menu, Save code, and send it with a note.
Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

mill.label: The mill town
mill.summary: Cotton and weaving sheds, the mill whistle at six. Half the men in your street joined the same week.

pit.label: The pit village
pit.summary: The colliery, the chapel and the club. You have worked underground since you were fourteen.

city.label: The city office
city.summary: A clerk's stool in a shipping office, a season ticket on the tram, and a rifle club on Saturdays.

farm.label: The farm village
farm.summary: Horses, hedges and a shotgun for the rooks. The harvest was in when the recruiting sergeant came.
